summary: 15 concise trial-paper-only hypotheses distilled from the ResearchAgent run for sprint, grouped by per-hypothesis feature attribution.

mechanisms.description: Higher baseline urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (uACR) increases the likelihood that an early eGFR decline represents intrinsic glomerular damage rather than a benign hemodynamic fall by indicating preexisting permeability and structural injury that predisposes to persistent loss of filtration.

Lower baseline creatinine‑ or cystatin C–based eGFR reflects reduced renal reserve and nephron mass, so the same magnitude of BP‑mediated perfusion reduction is more likely to cause irreversible injury and long‑term renal events.

Baseline diuretic use or higher diuretic exposure increases the risk that intensive BP lowering will precipitate renal hypoperfusion and ischemic tubular injury, making early eGFR declines more likely to be persistent and to predict sustained renal outcomes.

Elevated baseline urine NGAL normalized to creatinine indicates subclinical tubular injury that lowers the threshold for progression from an initial hemodynamic insult to frank tubular necrosis, so intensive BP lowering in these patients more often leads to persistent eGFR loss.

Higher baseline plasma cystatin C relative to creatinine suggests underestimated true GFR and reduced filtration capacity, increasing the probability that an early creatinine‑based eGFR drop reflects true loss of filtration rather than reversible creatinine kinetics.

Elevated baseline plasma renin or aldosterone denotes activated RAAS physiology that amplifies intrarenal hemodynamic shifts with intensive BP lowering, producing larger functional GFR changes that may either be reversible or, if extreme, precipitate tubular hypoperfusion and injury.

Black race, when accompanied by greater baseline hypertension‑related kidney structural change, predisposes to early eGFR declines that reflect preexisting structural injury and therefore a higher probability of persistent loss after intensive BP lowering.

Baseline discordance between cystatin C–based and creatinine‑based eGFR (cystatin C indicating worse GFR) identifies patients with lower true filtration reserve who are more likely to convert an early eGFR decline into sustained kidney function loss.

Baseline clinical atherosclerotic vascular disease reflects systemic microvascular and macrovascular stiffening that impairs renal autoregulation, so intensive BP reduction more readily leads to sustained reductions in GFR rather than transient hemodynamic changes.

Baseline anemia or low hemoglobin reduces renal oxygen delivery and predisposes the vulnerable medulla to ischemic tubular injury during episodes of intensive BP‑induced hypoperfusion, making early eGFR declines more likely to predict persistent renal outcomes.

Baseline use of ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy modifies the effect of intensive SBP lowering by dilating the efferent arteriole and lowering intraglomerular pressure, producing functional creatinine rises that are more often reversible unless accompanied by volume depletion or tubular injury.

Higher baseline NT‑proBNP or clinical markers of venous congestion identify a cardiorenal phenotype in which decongestion or rapid afterload reduction with intensive therapy can cause transient creatinine rises from redistribution of renal perfusion that are often reversible rather than intrinsic tubular injury.

Baseline elevated urine albumin‑creatinine ratio signals preexisting glomerular damage that increases the likelihood an early eGFR decline represents intrinsic kidney injury and predicts reduced renal benefit from continued intensive SBP lowering.

Older age is associated with impaired renal autoregulation and lower nephron reserve, so intensiv﻿e SBP lowering–related reductions in renal perfusion are more likely to produce structural ischemic injury and persistent decline rather than benign hemodynamic falls.

Presence of baseline albuminuria together with elevated tubular markers (e.g., NGAL or KIM‑1) indicates combined glomerular and tubular pathology that magnifies susceptibility to irreversible injury from intensive BP‑related perfusion changes, increasing long‑term renal event risk.
